No not with windows. There are complex cms systems that could do it but linux and to a certain extent windows are file based operating systems. Cms systems typically run on servers and will do things like store metadata and binary blobs in a db but typically run multiple instances on dedicated redundant servers.

Can't help you with the folders question but I'd give TestDisk a try. Its the most thorough tool I have used so far. It'll recover files into a directory of your choice. It will work best if you haven't done any write operations on the problem drive.

If your data matters that much to you, it is time to NAS or start paying for a cloud backup.

This is the inherent problem with external drive enclosures they have no fault tolerance.

Asking how to organize data on your PC without folders is like asking how to stock a warehouse or a library without shelves. It's silly, and it shows that you fundamentally don't understand how and why things work the way they do.

Folders didn't cause your data to be lost. A corrupted file allocation table did. Then you wrote to that corrupt file allocation table (renaming that one file) and it screwed things up further. The MP3 player not wanting to disconnect was just a symptom that Explorer was having issues with your external drive.

Sorry to hear you lost all your data. :( I'm surprised that Recuva wasn't able to find anything. While I've never used that software, I've used similar programs like GetDataBack for recovery. Did you try a really thorough deep scan of your drive to try and recover stuff? It takes an hour or two for the program to read every sector of the disk and try and interpret what everything is/was.

First off, your problem is that you wrote to the disk. You should've run chkdsk or data recovery software the instant you saw it was compromised.

On to your question, the answer is no. The way files are located in NTFS is by entries in a directory listing(ie, it's either in a folder or it's nowhere); it does support alternate data streams, but that's nothing like what you want.

What you're asking for is a tag-based file system; these do exist, but only experimentally. None have ever entered production use(and even if there was a production-quality one, it's doubtful a Windows driver would exist for it).
